abstract.p: This study highlights the benefits of Neglected and Underutilized crops (NUCs) by analyzing 56 peer-reviewed publications from different geographical locations. NUCs are climate resilient, can boost yields, expand nutritional diversity, empowerment, and livelihood status. Addressing poverty, hunger and malnutrition are global complex challenges requiring multiple perspectives and solutions; thus, NUC provides tremendous unexplored opportunities. This review connects the research gaps, strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities and provides recommendations for further exploration.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Several significant drivers, such as pandemics, climate change, wars, and rising inequality, have fueled the dramatic escalation of hunger and food insecurity worldwide since 20151. A core objective of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is to eradicate hunger and malnutrition by 2030, ensuring that all people, especially children, have year-round access to sufficient food2. The (SDG) 2: Zero Hunger focuses on “Achieving food security and improved nutrition, end hunger, and promote sustainable agriculture” along with eight subtargets3 (United Nations, 2024). Nutrition, agricultural, and food security practices are the main topics of the first five targets; the financial and market factors that make achieving those objectives easier are the focus of the final three targets4. Significant international occurrences (such as the Russia–Ukraine conflict, Israel–Palestine conflict, and the COVID-19 pandemic) have led to a significant regression of the progress in achieving SDG2, returning to levels recorded in 20154. While some countries have made progress, most are not on course to fulfill the targets by 2030. In the year 2020, for example, the worldwide trend of undernourishment prevalence (goal 2.1.1) returned to 2009–2010 levels5 as a consequence of the COVID-19 outbreak’s several shocks to the food systems. The prior upward trend in the rates of childhood stunting (goal 2.2.1) was broken after 2020 when the levels stagnated. In a similar vein, the trend of declining prevalence of wasting gave way to a standstill, while the proportion of overweight people even somewhat grew (goal 2.2.2)6. There were 2.4 billion people on the earth in 2022, roughly 29.6% of the total population who were food insecure to a moderate degree. Of them, 11.3% of the global population, or 900 million people, suffered from severe food insecurity. 600 million people are expected to be chronically malnourished by 2030, according to updated FIES-based projections of the prevalence of food insecurity. The global fight against food insecurity made little progress in 2022. While there has been some progress in reducing hunger in Asia and Latin America between 2021 and 2022, hunger is still increasing in Western Asia, the Caribbean, and every subregion of Africa7.

Not only are the pandemic and war responsible for this alarming situation but also our current methods of producing and food consumption is one of the main causes of health issues worldwide and hurt the ecosystem. With over 500 million undernourished people living in Asia and 250 million in Africa, the world is not on track to meet SDG2, which calls for the eradication of hunger by 20308. The fact that the food system is not sustainable at the local, state, federal, or global levels is alarming. Emerging pandemics, climate change, depletion of natural resources, and intermittent conflicts have highlighted the shortcomings of food systems in providing wholesome and secure food9. At one end of the scale, farming will need to be intensified to satisfy the need for food by 9 billion individuals. However, if any kind of long-term food security is to be achieved, local concerns like dietary diversity and nutritional deficiencies will also need to be addressed10. Enhancing ecosystem services is necessary to shift to more sustainable agricultural landscapes and food systems, which calls for transformative techniques. This is an Integrative Review, covering literature across multiple themes (Agriculture, food and nutrition, environment, gender, policy). The goal is to achieve sustainable human health and well-being as well as social, ecological, and economic results11,12. One strategy to support sustainable transition is to use underutilized crops to diversify agricultural landscapes, food systems, and diets13. The purpose of this analysis is to conduct a critical analysis of the possibility of integrating underutilized crops into mainstream agricultural systems as a strategic option to enhance diverse sources of food, improve food and nutrition security, combat environmental concerns, and strengthen agricultural resilience to climate variability.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p:
A literature search was done by using the databases of PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Subject headings terms were “Underutilized Crops,” “Neglected Underutilized Crops,” “Sustainable Food System,” and “Case Studies.” Research paper reference lists were also reviewed. English language research paper was included in this study. The search strategy can be found in Fig. 114.Fig. 1
Literature search on neglected underutilized crops (NUCs).

sec.title: Study selection criteria
sec.p: An eligibility criterion was established before the screening process. Only those studies that contain—(1) Information about underutilized crops was included; (2) Emphasis was given to recently published research articles (mostly those which were published between 2000 and 2024); (3) Those studies that contain successful case stories on underutilized crops were added to show the significance of underutilized crops, and also the lack that is found in the study is included.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: Every piece of qualitative and quantitative data from publications that qualified was incorporated into the study process. Data were taken from the design, subjects, intervention, and outcomes of each included study (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Sustainable food system: for achieving zero hunger
sec.p: For human growth, sustainability has emerged as a key theory and objective15. To achieve sustainable development, everyone’s basic requirements must be met, and everyone must have the chance to realize their dreams of a better life16. A sustainable food system provides food and nutrition security for all while maintaining the social, economic, and environmental foundations necessary to provide nutrition and food security for future generations. There are several complex and interconnected obstacles facing efforts to improve global food security10. The scenario is unsustainable because of the ongoing climate change, the limited amount of water accessible, and energy constraints8. Furthermore, it is not sufficient to just produce enough food; it also needs to be gathered, processed, and distributed, and the impoverished need to be able to afford it to have access to this food supply10. To guarantee everyone’s future food security, it is imperative to implement more diverse agricultural systems and food sources, and this might potentially restore nearly 75% of the genetic loss of crop diversity during the process17. Using underappreciated and neglected crop species to diversify food systems, agricultural landscapes and diet pattern could be one tactic to assist such a shift11,12.

There are currently only thirty species that are farmed for food, with six crops—rice, wheat, maize, potato, soybean, and sugarcane—sharing more than seventy-five percent of the energy obtained from plants. Due to the introduction of high-yielding wheat and rice varieties and the excessive application of soil nitrogen, Asia saw a “green revolution” that increased the percentage of undernourished people from one in three in 1960 to about one in ten now. However, agricultural diversity in underdeveloped nations has suffered since the start of the green revolution18. Now, Super-nutrient foods are no longer grown because higher-yielding crops provide more calories. A sedentary lifestyle combined with an excess of refined carbohydrates raises the risk of glucotoxicity, a condition connected to a higher risk of non-communicable diseases (NCDs)19. Underutilized or neglected crops can play a big role in increased food security in a variety of ways. Neglected and underutilized crops offer tremendous opportunities to fight hunger, malnutrition, and poverty. They can also help build climate-resilient, nutrient-dense, and sustainable agriculture when incorporated into farming systems20. To counteract malnutrition, which encompasses both overnutrition and undernutrition, a good diet is crucial. Protein, fats, energy, fiber, and essential nutrients like fatty acids, amino acids, carbs, minerals, vitamins, and fluids are all provided in sufficient amounts and variety by an adequate diet to promote healthy growth and lower the risk of food-related illnesses20. A diet low in nutrients, particularly foods lacking in micronutrients, is the main risk factor for the global burden of diseases, which is thought to impact 3 billion people globally8. It is generally accepted that changes must be made to the current food systems to make them more resilient, sustainable, and egalitarian to achieve food and nutritional security11,12.

sec.title: Significance of neglected and underutilized crops (NUCs)
sec.p: Food is characterized as NUCs (Neglected and Underutilized Crops) that are rich in nutrients, resilient to climate change, commercially feasible, and available locally or with adaptability20. Underutilized and neglected crops supply vital macronutrients like proteins, fats, and carbohydrates; micronutrients like vitamins and minerals; and bioactive non-nutrients that promote health21. However, for a variety of socioeconomic or political reasons, many of these nutrient-rich traditional cultivars have fallen into dereliction. Sustainable agriculture depends on agrobiodiversity, and underutilized crops are a vital component to support sustainable agri-food systems20. Worldwide, an estimated 30,000 kinds of edible plants have been found, with over 7000 of those being grown for human use22. Even more alarming is the fact that 90% of the food required for the globe has been generated by just 20 species, with 60% of the human diet consisting of wheat, maize, and rice23. Because of this, tens of thousands of edible plant species are still largely “underutilized” in terms of their potential to help feed the world’s growing hungry population23. Only 103 of the 150 plant species that are currently commercially cultivated provide 90% of the calories in the human diet24. For many years, for a variety of genetic, agronomic, social, cultural, and economic reasons, farmers, researchers, food producers, traders, and consumers, and governments ignored the majority of these crops25. Some crop varieties were lost before they had a chance to be studied, described, grown, and advertised, together with a wealth of information about how to grow and use them26.

There are two primary categories of crops: underutilized and staple. The majority of underused crops are native or partially native plants that have adapted to their specific environments. They are also called little-used, promising, neglected, minor orphans27. The crops that had been traditional staples for generations were increasingly neglected after farming systems acquired access to more productive crops20. Underutilized crops can help us in several ways: (1) A targeted initiative to assist the underprivileged with income and subsistence; (2) A strategy to lessen the danger of being overly dependent on a small number of important crops; (3) An approach to boost agricultural sustainability by lowering inputs, such as fertilizers and fuel derived from fossil fuels, considering the hazards associated with agriculture’s carbon imprint on climate change and the shift to a post-peak-oil society; (4) An enhancement of food quality and a means of celebrating and protecting nutritional and cultural variety.

sec.title: Nutritional and environmental benefits of neglected and underutilized crops (NUCs)
sec.p:
Promoting the utilization of underutilized crops is primarily beneficial because of their enormous nutritional significance in alleviating hidden hunger18. Underutilized crops are believed to have higher nutritional content than conventional crops, and they may even be able to assist the United Nations’ second Sustainable Development Goal (SDG), which is to end hunger. In terms of nutrition, the majority of underutilized crops are superior to staple crops26. Compared to modern types of rice and wheat, millets, chia, and quinoa have several times greater carbohydrate quality with abundant dietary fiber sources and high-quality protein sources with enriched essential amino acids28. In addition to being important for local populations’ survival, several of these traditional crops have unique social, cultural, and medicinal values. In contrast to most staple crops, NUCs frequently provide sustainable food production because they are well-suited to the difficult and marginal local growth circumstances. Improved sustainability23, less input consumption, and increased food systems’ shock resistance are additional ways that NUCs have an impact30. It is reported that NUCs are more drought and heat-stress-tolerant than common staple crops12. By cultivating crops that are naturally immune to specific pests and illnesses, NUCs may also help the environment by reducing the need for irrigation and water waste. Through reducing the application of hazardous chemical pesticides, NUCs contribute to breeding crops that endure drought conditions17. It will be necessary to generate and disseminate this knowledge more quickly than was done for main crops if NUCs are predicted to play a key role as future crops in irrigation-limited environments23. When it comes to consistent yields in poor soils and unfavorable climate conditions, NUCs are more resilient to biotic and abiotic stressors than main staple food crops26. In addition to offering a range of nutrient-dense food sources that can increase food security and lower hunger and malnutrition globally, diversification in agricultural production systems using more resilient NUCs can considerably lessen the effects of climate change31. Land and water are two of the scarce resources needed to produce more food to feed the world’s growing population. The growing number of people on land due to population increase presents a significant obstacle to reversing the food insecurity that exists in many regions of the world. This frequently results in actions that might not be environmentally friendly or sustainable, including the careless application of artificial fertilizers, which can have unfavorable consequences on the environment like water pollution, global warming, soil erosion, and climate change32. The consequences of recurrent water shortages and erratic droughts brought on by environmental change are extremely detrimental31. “Sustainable intensification” is needed to increase food production from the same amount of land while minimizing negative environmental effects33. Argo-biodiversity-focused and environmentally friendly agricultural practices can increase the availability and accessibility of underutilized foods that can help reduce micronutrient shortages, particularly in rural tropical areas. NUCs can support a diverse and healthy diet both at the species level and at the level of variation within a species. sec.title: Cultural and social significance
sec.p:
While the global significance of NUCs is still unknown, nations in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and South and East Asia believe it to be of moderate to medium importance34. Asian nations with high NUCs usage include India, Malaysia, Nepal, and the Philippines; those with moderate NUCs use include Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and Sri Lanka35. In recent years, young people’s eating habits have been impacted by cultural shifts. The impact of increasingly Westernized diets is to blame for this. Customers and traditional food cultures are not connected, and this situation is further exacerbated by the belief that traditional crops are outdated and unappealing in comparison to modern ones. Lower-income nations are also seeing an increase in the consumption of baked and fried foods. The average individual nowadays consumes three times the daily recommended amount of salt and sugar, typically in the form of soft drinks or snacks27. Data from ref. 36 provides a visual depiction of dietary patterns, food security inequalities, and agricultural diversity worldwide. These maps show the areas where NUCs have a major impact on local food systems by highlighting the unequal distribution of staple crops and NUCs. The information also highlights the effects of Westernized dietary changes, especially in lower-income countries where processed foods are gradually replacing traditional eating habits. Furthermore, the spatial trends in agricultural participation correspond with the function of NUCs in bolstering rural livelihoods, especially for women, who are essential to the production, gathering, and consumption of food (Fig. 2).Fig. 2
Geographical agricultural diversity representation and NUCs’ function in food systems.

Poor rural farming families use NUCs for revenue generation, medicine, and consumption37. Rural people can grow these crops more if they sell more. By this, they can be able to improve their income. Underutilized crops can be especially essential for empowering women since in various societies, males focus on producing commercial and staple crops, while women are primary caretakers of these crops and the traditional knowledge that goes along with them37,38. In addition to overseeing the family diet, women frequently perform important roles in food cultivation, collection, preparation, and storage. They support equitable, long-term, and sustainable economic growth as well as full-time, productive employment and respectable jobs for all37. Promoting and encouraging the use of underused crops in local cuisines may lead to an increase in their consumption as well as a rise in the number of farmers growing them to fulfill market demand and enhance food security, livelihoods, and human nutrition32. Advertising diversity in local, national, and global markets won’t work unless people know about it and are prepared to pay for goods that promote diversity28.

sec.title: SWOT analysis of the NUCs
sec.p:
SWOT analysis is a strategic planning tool used to identify Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. It helps in assessing both internal and external factors to guide decision-making and strategy development. Finding out which internal (strengths and weaknesses) and external (threats and opportunities) factors are beneficial or unfavorable for the NUCs is the goal of a SWOT analysis. There are excellent SWOT analyses from the literature review37,39, providing an overview from farm to fork in a 2*2 SWOT matrix. This review summarizes the SWOT table39 content into four categories: Agriculture (A), Processing (P), Consumer (C), and Government (G). The SWOT matrices focused more on the farm level and the consumer level; the middle segment of the food supply chain (processing) is not clearly addressed. This review provides a SWOT tree diagram focusing on the middle segment, which is a critical missing gap to develop a sustainable food system model (Fig. 3).Fig. 3
SWOT analysis of neglected and underutilized crops (NUCs).

sec.title: Barriers and challenges
sec.p: Despite being far more nutritious and occasionally outperforming most conventional crops, Neglected and Underutilized Crops (NUCs) are not fully included in our current food systems. Even with growing knowledge of their nutritional benefits, there are still a lot of obstacles to overcome. There are some challenges which include environmental, economic, social, political, and agronomic challenges in exploring the potentials of NUCs17.

There is a misconception that NUCs are “poor man’s crops,” foods connected to starvation or difficult times30,61. Many people have a preference barrier associated with consumption and a poor perception of NUCs. Many of the indigenous, traditional crop species and variations have been replaced by high-yielding staple crop cultivars created by contemporary breeding initiatives as a result of the Green Revolution29. Considering that NUCs usually fall short of modern standards for uniformity and other attributes, as well as the fact that breeders in both the public and private sectors tend to overlook them, NUCs are typically less competitive in the market than commercial cultivars.

The barriers are also a part of a wider perspective that is fundamentally changing how we live, such as urbanization, the rise of large corporations over smaller farms, and the homogenization of local cultures because of the spread of staple crops40. The major difficulties that individuals who manage and safeguard NUCs must overcome are well documented in the Second Report on the Status of the World’s Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (FAO, 2010)41. These difficulties, which span a variety of domains including social, economic, and environmental ones, are presented in Table 4 (Note: Term “neglected” highlights the lack of attention or focus on a particular subject, while “underutilized” emphasizes that something, though known and available, is not being used to its full potential).Table 4

Conversely, neglected and underutilized crops are being used as cover crops42 have seen a major gain in market value in recent years. An increasing number of individuals are including these crops in their meals as they become more conscious of their beneficial effects on the environment and nutritional worth. Influential people like celebrities and social media influencers are a major force behind this trend; they progressively support and incorporate these crops into their lives. An increased number of people are exploring underutilized crops due to these public individuals’ encouragement via social media and other venues. As a result, despite these crops’ potential to improve food security, there is a greater demand for them in certain groups, which has driven up their prices. Table 5 summarizes areas of action along with proposed initiatives to support food sustainability with NUCs. This review proposes a model for a sustainable solution based on the information and consolidation of strategies from existing knowledge on NUCs. For mainstreaming underutilized crops into the agricultural and policy system, a holistic approach is needed from the grassroots level for all the approaches to be interlinked. sec.title: Conclusion: cultivating a food-secure, sustainable future
sec.p: The integration of underutilized crops into modern food systems is challenged by inconsistent quality, limited processing and standardization, and unclear regulations on novel foods and health claims. There are multiple factors that collectively hinder their wider adoption despite their nutritional and ecological value. The existing food system is ecologically unstable, largely depending on a small number of crops. Our food system is currently at a turning point, and the earth’s vitality is increasingly depleted from feeding billions of people. Our dishes bear the burden of unsustainable decisions as well as the tales of distant nations, monocultures, diverse species loss and lost cuisines. Our destination should be an equitable table where biodiversity is respected in the seeds we sow, the Earth and our bodies are nourished by every bite, and the futures being cultivated are ones characterized by justice, compassion, and an appreciation for the interconnectedness of all living things (from soil to humans). However, the key to a thriving future lies in a diverse tapestry of underutilized crops. These forgotten treasures can revolutionize agriculture, leading us into an era of food security and environmental balance. This goes beyond simply replacing existing crops; it involves creating a more diverse agricultural symphony, cultivating a stunning mosaic of resilience and variety. The benefits will extend far beyond our plates, reaching multiple generations yet to come. These agricultural transformations can become the foundation of climate-smart farming, supporting regenerative agriculture. By embracing underutilized crops, we can break free from the limitations of monoculture and embrace the potential of biodiversity. It means exploring the unique attributes of neglected crops and integrating them into our agricultural practices. It means diversifying our fields and embracing the richness that nature has to offer. By doing this, we may develop a food system that feeds the world, nutritiously, robustly, and sustainably. It’s time to shift our focus from the familiar to the forgotten.
